title: Interface as Bounds
concept: Interfaces serve as bounds on type parameters — T: Eq means 'T must implement the Eq interface', restricting what types can be used.
why: Interface bounds are how the compiler knows what operations are available on generic types. Without bounds, you can't call any methods on T.
tips: Interface bounds ARE your function's requirements — they document what the type must support
Start with minimal bounds and add more as the compiler tells you what's missing
Read bounds as: 'This function works with any T that is Clone AND Display'
The compiler is your ally — it tells you exactly which interface you forgot to require
common_mistakes: Adding bounds you don't use (e.g., T: Display but never calling to_str)
Forgetting bounds until the compiler complains — think ahead about what operations you need
Using overly restrictive bounds (T: Clone + Copy + Display + Debug + Ord + Hash) when T: Ord suffices
